idiom_name: struct with canned-answer methods satisfying the interface implicitly
implementation_notes: Go needs no mocking runtime: interfaces are satisfied implicitly (go.dev/ref/spec, Interface types), so a stub is an ordinary struct whose methods return the canned value, valid the moment it has the right method set. Define the interface where it is consumed, keep it narrow, and pass the stub where the production code expects the interface; the compile-time assertion var _ Warehouse = (*stubWarehouse)(nil) turns interface drift into a build error instead of a silent test failure. testify's mock.Mock and uber's gomock/mockgen generate the same answers plus call expectations, which is what to reach for when the interface is large or the interaction itself must be asserted; for a plain canned answer the hand-written struct is shorter, faster to read and adds no dependency.
pitfalls: A value receiver copies the stub into the interface, so state a test expects to observe after the call must sit behind a pointer receiver or a pointer field.
Adding a method to a consumer-side interface breaks every hand-written stub; keep the interface at the consumer and add the compile-time assertion so breakage is loud.
A stub shared by parallel subtests is shared mutable state - give each subtest its own value, guard the fields, and run the suite with -race.

variants.name: testify mock with On(...).Return(...)
variants.idiom_name: testify mock.Mock embedded in a hand-written type + On/Return
variants.implementation_notes: testify's mock package is a small library that tracks activity on another object: embed mock.Mock in a type that implements the interface, forward each method through m.Called(args...), and programme answers with m.On("HasInventory", "Talisker", 50).Return(false). It generates no code, so the wrapper is still hand-written, but argument matching, per-call cardinality and AssertExpectations come for free - useful when a test needs both canned answers and a check of what was called. uber's gomock/mockgen is the other common route (code-generated from the interface, with a controller that verifies at test end); reach for either when the interface is large or several tests share the same programmed answers, and keep the assertion style deliberate so the double stays a stub rather than an implicit mock.
pitfalls: A method that was called without a matching On() panics, so every method the SUT touches needs a programmed answer even when the test does not care about it.
AssertExpectations is mock semantics: calling it converts the stub into an interaction test and makes harmless refactorings fail.
m.Called must be called inside each wrapper method; forgetting one returns zero values silently and the test passes against the wrong answer.
